# Mahākaṇhajātaka (Ja 469)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahākaṇhajātaka* (Ja 469) is a narrative belonging to the *Dvādasanipāta* (Book of Twelves) of the Pali Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1877; Fausböll 1887]. The canonical verse section opens with the words *Kaṇho kaṇho ca* ("A black, black hound") [Fausböll 1887]. According to the commentary, the setting for the telling of the tale is the Jetavana monastery, where the Buddha discourses on living for the benefit of the world (*lokatthacariyā*) [Fausböll 1887]. In the introductory episode (*paccuppannavatthu*), the monks praise the Buddha's tireless compassion in converting difficult individuals such as Aṅgulimāla and his journeying to teach the first five disciples [Fausböll 1887; Monius 2001; Clark 1994].

In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), the Bodhisatta is born as the god Sakka, who intervenes in an irreligious world accompanied by his celestial charioteer Mātali and a giant hound (*mahākaṇha*), terrifying people into abandoning evil and establishing them in generosity and moral conduct (*dānasīla*) [Fausböll 1887; Fausböll 1897; Harris 2006]. Through this intervention, Sakka enables the religious dispensation (*sāsana*) to endure for another thousand years [Fausböll 1887]. In the identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the Buddha reveals that Mātali was Ānanda and Sakka was the Bodhisatta himself [Fausböll 1887].

 DharmaNexus detects substantial Pali-internal text reuse between the canonical verses and the commentary (*Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, fourth volume), encompassing eight matching segments (spanning §2.4–12.4 of the text) [DharmaNexus]. In secondary literature and earlier translations, the introductory framework of the *Mahākaṇhajātaka* is frequently cross-referenced by other tales sharing the theme of *lokatthacariyā* [Fausböll 1877; Cowell 1897], and an early English rendering was published in the nineteenth century under the pen name Philalethes [Harris 2006].
